html.p: Welcome to Lecture 1: Linear Regression & the Statistical Sommelier (Supervised Learning), taught by Professor Dimitris Bertsimas, Boeing Leaders for Global Operations Professor of Management and Professor of Operations Research at MIT. In this lecture, we explore one of the most fundamental tools in machine learning and statistics: linear regression. To bring the concept to life, we consider an unconventional but fascinating application—predicting the quality of Bordeaux wines.

Traditionally, expert sommeliers evaluate wine vintages based on taste and experience. But can data and quantitative models provide equally accurate or even superior predictions? In the early 1990s, Princeton economist Orley Ashenfelter stirred controversy by showing that simple linear regression models, using weather and aging variables, could predict wine quality and prices with surprising accuracy. His approach challenged the authority of world-famous critics, sparking debate in both the wine industry and the statistical community.

This example illustrates a broader theme: how quantitative models can disrupt domains dominated by subjective judgment. It sets the stage for our deeper dive into the mechanics, intuition, and power of linear regression.
By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:

ol.li: Understand the basics of linear regression: Learn how linear regression models predict a continuous outcome variable based on independent variables.
Apply linear regression to real-world problems: Use linear regression to predict wine quality based on factors like age, temperature, and rainfall.
Interpret regression coefficients: Understand how to interpret the coefficients in a linear regression model and their significance.
Evaluate model performance: Learn how to use metrics like R² and Sum of Squared Errors (SSE) to assess the performance of a linear regression model.
Compare models to expert opinions: Understand how quantitative models can outperform traditional expert judgments in certain domains.

html.p: Welcome to Supervised and Unsupervised Learning! This module explores both supervised and unsupervised learning, both important aspects of machine learning.

Supervised learning is at the heart of modern machine learning. In supervised learning, models are trained on datasets where the outcomes (or “labels”) are already known, allowing us to make predictions for future cases. This module introduces the foundations of supervised learning through four diverse and real-world applications that together show how supervised learning enables us to predict outcomes, evaluate model performance, and inform real-world decisions across medicine, law, and beyond.

ul.li: Linear regression (The Statistical Sommelier) – predicting Bordeaux wine quality using weather and aging data.
Logistic regression (The Framingham Heart Study) – predicting the 10-year risk of heart disease based on patient risk factors.
Decision trees (The Supreme Court) – using interpretable tree-based models to forecast Supreme Court rulings.
Logistic regression in healthcare (Predicting Quality in Healthcare) – scaling expert assessments to evaluate patient care quality using claims data.

html.p: Unsupervised learning focuses on uncovering hidden structures in data where labels are not available. Instead of predicting outcomes, the goal is to find meaningful patterns, groupings, or representations that make complex data easier to understand and act upon. This module introduces unsupervised learning through the lens of clustering, a method for grouping similar observations:

ul.li: Foundations of Clustering – You will learn how k-means and hierarchical clustering organize data into meaningful groups, why normalization is essential when features are on different scales, and how tools like scree plots help determine the right number of clusters. Real-world examples—from customer segmentation to patient health profiles—demonstrate how clustering transforms raw data into actionable insights.

Interpretable Clustering – You will see how clustering results can be made transparent and actionable. By combining k-means clustering with Optimal Classification Trees (OCT), complex groupings can be explained through simple, rule-based profiles (e.g., “Female Commuters,” “Weekend Riders,” “Short Rides”). This approach bridges the gap between machine-generated clusters and human understanding, enabling decisions in marketing, planning, and customer engagement.

html.p: Together, these lectures show how unsupervised learning allows us to uncover patterns without labels and transform them into strategies that managers, clinicians, and policymakers can readily use.

Each lecture comes with a downloadable PDF slide deck that maps directly to the visual materials shown in the video. These files are designed as an alternative study aid to read the detail of key text, math, and graphics shown in the video
By the end of this module, students will be able to:

ol.li: Understand the role of data and analytics in decision-making: Learn how data-driven approaches can improve decision-making in various domains, from sports to healthcare.
Apply statistical and machine learning models: Gain hands-on experience with models like linear regression, logistic regression, and decision trees.
Interpret model results: Learn how to interpret coefficients, odds ratios, and tree splits to make informed decisions.
Evaluate model performance: Understand how to use metrics like R², AUC, and accuracy to assess model performance.
Compare models to traditional approaches: Learn how data-driven models can complement or outperform traditional methods, such as expert opinions or subjective assessments.
Define and apply clustering methods: Understand the role of clustering in unsupervised learning, and learn how k-means and hierarchical clustering group data points into meaningful segments.
Prepare and normalize data for clustering: Recognize why scaling and normalization are essential for fair comparisons across features with different units.
Determine the number of clusters: Use tools such as scree plots to identify the “sweet spot” for distinct and actionable groupings.
Interpret and communicate clusters: Analyze centroids, dendrograms, and segmentation outputs to describe patterns in the data.
Make clusters interpretable: Combine clustering with Optimal Classification Trees (OCT) to generate transparent, rule-based profiles that decision-makers can easily understand and apply.
